opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think PromptBreeder is interesting less for the specific benchmark numbers and more for what it hints at. The core idea is simple. You have a population of task prompts, and you use the language model itself to mutate and improve them. The twist is that the mutation prompts, the instructions telling the model *how* to improve a prompt, are also evolved. So the system improves its solutions and also, to some degree, the process by which it improves them. That self-referential loop is what excites me.

If you squint, that's a tiny version of what science is. Scientists don't just generate hypotheses and test them. Over time they also refine how they generate hypotheses, which methods to try, and which questions are worth asking. PromptBreeder is a very constrained sandbox for that, but it shows that language models can act as a mutation operator over ideas, not just random perturbations. They have a sense of what a meaningful variation looks like, because they've absorbed so much human knowledge about what's interesting.

That connects to the broader open-endedness agenda that I care a lot about. For a long time the bottleneck in open-ended systems was that we didn't have good ways to generate interesting novelty or to judge what's interesting. Foundation models give us a handle on both. So you can imagine moving from evolving prompts to evolving code, experiments, and eventually research directions. The system proposes something, runs it, evaluates it, and feeds that back in. We're starting to see early versions of that kind of AI-scientist loop.

I'd add some caveats. In PromptBreeder there's a clear fitness signal, you have a benchmark and you can measure accuracy. Real science is much messier. Often the hardest part is knowing what's worth pursuing before you have a metric for it. And there's the risk of overfitting or Goodharting whatever evaluator you put in the loop. So I don't think we've automated research. But I do think we've shown that the self-improvement loop can be put into natural language and driven by the model itself. That's a meaningful step toward systems that keep discovering things on their own rather than just optimizing a fixed objective we hand them.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes PromptBreeder as a constrained, “tiny version” of science and connects evolving prompts to automating scientific research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think PromptBreeder is interesting less for what it does on any particular benchmark and more for what it points at. The core idea is that you have a language model, and you want it to get better at some task, and rather than a human sitting there hand-crafting prompts and trying things out, you let an evolutionary process do that search. You have a population of task prompts, you evaluate them on the task, you keep the ones that do well, and you mutate them using the language model itself. And the part I find most exciting is that the mutation prompts, the instructions that tell the model how to change a prompt, are themselves evolved. So it's self-referential. The system is improving the way it improves itself.

Now, why does that matter for scientific research? I think the way to see it is that a lot of what makes science slow is this outer loop. You have a hypothesis, you design an experiment, you run it, you look at the results, and then a human has to come back and say, okay, what should I try next? And that step of deciding what to try next is where a lot of the creativity and a lot of the bottleneck sits. What PromptBreeder shows, in a very narrow setting, is that you can close that loop. The model generates candidates, the candidates get evaluated against something objective, and the model also generates better ways of generating candidates. You don't need a human in the inner loop anymore.

I want to be careful not to oversell it. PromptBreeder is operating on prompts for well-defined tasks where you have a clear fitness signal, something like accuracy on GSM8K. Science mostly doesn't look like that. The hard part of science is often that you don't know what the right objective is, or the evaluation is extremely expensive, or it takes a wet lab. So I don't think PromptBreeder is automating science. But I do think it's an existence proof for a particular pattern, which is open-ended search where the language model is both the thing being improved and the thing driving the improvement. And that pattern, combined with better evaluation, better tools, and the ability to actually run experiments, is what I think will eventually matter for research automation.

The other thing I'd say is that it fits into this broader thread of open-endedness that I care a lot about. Evolution is the only process we know of that actually produced general intelligence, and it did that without a fixed objective. It just kept generating novel, interesting things. Language models give us a mutation operator that's actually sensible, that proposes variations which are meaningful rather than random. So when you combine that with a selection pressure, you get something that starts to look like a very primitive version of a scientific community: lots of ideas, most of them bad, a few surviving and getting refined. I think that's the direction, and PromptBreeder is one small, concrete step along it.

r002.rationale: It describes PromptBreeder as a narrow existence proof of a pattern that could matter for research automation, while noting that it does not automate science broadly.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing about PromptBreeder is that it’s a small step toward systems that can improve the way they search for solutions. You’re evolving prompts, but you’re also evolving the prompts that produce changes to those prompts. So the search procedure itself becomes something you can optimize.

There’s an interesting connection to scientific research there. We don’t just want systems that generate candidate answers; we want systems that can propose hypotheses, design experiments, evaluate the results, and use that feedback to decide what to try next. Potentially, they could also improve those research strategies over time.

But I wouldn’t equate improving prompts on a benchmark with automating science. The difficult part is getting reliable feedback: how do you establish that a hypothesis is actually useful or that an experiment tells you something new? PromptBreeder explores one mechanism that might contribute to that broader loop. It’s a promising direction, rather than a complete solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about PromptBreeder is that it starts to automate part of the process of deciding how to search for a solution. You’re evolving prompts, but you’re also evolving the prompts that produce those variations. So the system can improve the way it explores, rather than relying entirely on a strategy that a human has specified upfront.

There’s a connection there to scientific research: we propose hypotheses, test them, and use the results to decide what to investigate next. You could imagine systems that help automate more of that cycle, including generating candidate ideas and refining experimental strategies.

But I wouldn’t equate improving prompts with doing science autonomously. The crucial question is whether you have a reliable way to test an idea. A system can get very good at optimizing a particular score without producing a meaningful discovery. So I see this as an interesting step toward that broader ambition, with evaluation and grounding in experiments still absolutely central.
